 Sedgwick offers advice on preparing for food safety recalls and what could come in 2027. Dave Fusaro Nov. 18, 2026 3 min read Add Us On Google 
 148050380 © Alexander Raths | Dreamstime.com 6afe03fe7c5b4a4b473f04b3 Foodsafetydreamstime S 148050380 1 Edited Five risk categories account for 87% of U.S. food and drink recall activity so far this year, according to Sedgwick: undeclared allergens, bacterial contamination, foreign material, non-bacterial contamination and mislabeling.
 “While these may appear to be distinct hazards, together they point to a broader issue: the resilience of the systems and controls underpinning food and drink production,” said an analysis and report from Sedgwick, a global administrator of claims, benefits, loss adjusting and product recall.
 “A single quality failure can quickly move beyond the point of origin, affecting production, supply continuity, consumer safety and brand trust.”
 U.S. food and drink recall activity has remained elevated over the past five years, according to the firm. Events increased from 328 in Q1-Q3 2022 to 389 in the same period of 2026, despite notable year-to-year fluctuations and peaks in 2023 and 2025.
 Recall activity in 2026 remains 19% above 2022 levels, despite intervening fluctuations. “This sustained elevation suggests that manufacturers must prepare for a risk environment in which recalls remain a persistent operational consideration, rather than an exceptional disruption,” the report says.
 Recall exposure is markedly different depending on the products manufactured. The leading product categories this year show distinct combinations of allergen, bacterial contamination, foreign material, quality and other risks.
 Start with understanding where exposure is concentrated across your own products, ingredients, suppliers, manufacturing processes and quality systems. “Rather than relying on broader industry benchmarks … use sector intelligence to identify where [your] risk profile aligns with, or diverges from, the wider market.
 “Quality and safety failures can prompt questions well beyond the affected product itself,” the report continues. “The robustness of supplier controls, ingredient traceability, manufacturing processes, investigations and quality governance can increasingly determine how an event develops and how extensively it must be managed.”
 As for what to prepare for in 2027, “the past five years provide valuable perspective on where food and drink recalls have originated [but] they do not provide a definitive roadmap for what comes next.
 “FDA and USDA regulatory environments continue to evolve, while supply chains and ingredient networks become more complex. At the same time, organizations face greater pressure to maintain product availability, even as safety concerns demand rapid and effective action.”
 Sedgwick offers three bullet points for the new year:
 Use external intelligence to challenge internal assumptions.
 Expect greater scrutiny around the systems behind the product.
 Test the organization, not just the recall plan.
